The resin is carried on a polyethylene film so it does not make direct contact with the belt. The cut fibers fall on the resin coming in from the bottom, and then get covered by the resin coming in from the top – hence the fibers are sandwiched between resin films. The chopped fibers are hence wet with thermoset resin fed in the doctor boxes – i.e., unsaturated polyester, epoxy, vinyl ester or phenolic resin. The sandwich of the resin-fiber-resin passes through series of compaction rollers during which the resin works its way to wet out the fibers at the filament level. The material exits from the compaction roller and falls into open cardboard box in the form of an accordion configuration. This is illustrated in Figure 1. The intermediate product is a tacky discontinuous randomly oriented sheet. The SMC ‘charge’ used for compression molding is cut out of these intermediate sheet(s).The SMC ‘charge’ has a shelf life of approximately six weeks. Within that the sheet is cut to size and placed in a two-cavity compression mold. The mold is compressed at 1000-1200 psi and the charge flows under heat and pressure to fill the mold cavity to produce the final near net shape part. An industrial line has series of inlet tanks that carry the ingredients as shown in the figure. At the lab scale, these are mixed homogenously in a mixer and conveyed manually to the doctor boxes. It may be noted that all the work reported here is conducted under these constraints. Technical challenges addressed in this project There is a significant need to expand material options for SMC that has traditionally used glass fibers for decades. There are several integral issues related to chopping and conveying a range of materials including glass, carbon, basalt, thermoplastic tapes, and recycled fibers. These are in a variety of forms including continuous tows, discontinuous agglomerates such as pyrolyzed carbon fibers that could be used to produce a range of SMC intermediates. Standard/conventional SMC processing is limited to cutting rotors specifically for glass and compounding with thermoset polyesters and some epoxies.
